item.title: Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz89w59l3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas - Published It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region. In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police. "This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much. "If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day." Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" – a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east. However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it. The full capture of Donbas, made up of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, is a key objective for Russia. Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Russian army already controls almost all of Luhansk region, and is now in control of almost 80% of Donetsk region too, where all three fortress cities lie. For the past few months, the territory near Kramatorsk and Slovyansk has been the main focus of Russian ground assaults. Capturing them would potentially make it much easier for Russia to advance to the west. The two cities are now facing intense strikes from drones and bombs. Many civilians have already left, and key streets there are now covered with anti-drone nets, says Viktor Makurin, a volunteer from London. "There are often [remote-controlled] FPV drones in the air, you can hear them through the window. Driving around the city is lethally dangerous. There are drones lying in ambush on the roads, too," he told the BBC. "You can always hear explosions in the background, plus there are mobile groups firing at drones." Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police. Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August. Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction". The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC. One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say. Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk. Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal. Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg. "The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko. "Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media. "They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?" Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists. What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin. In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it. He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas. "Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month. Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands. "There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said. "What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding."

item.title: 'We never recovered him': Quest to identify remains from Ground Zero continues
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8d37gq1jnlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'We never recovered him': Quest to identify remains from Ground Zero continues - Published For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life is his mangled firefighter helmet. Scauso's father, Dennis - part of a New York City Fire Department (FDNY) hazmat unit for 12 years - initially was not scheduled to work on 11 September, 2001, but switched shifts for the overtime pay. The Long Island father of four was likely in the South Tower of the World Trade Center when it collapsed, the Scauso family was told. The helmet with his badge number was found months later. "I've spent essentially my entire life knowing my father died, and learning to live with the fact that we never recovered him," said Scauso, who was four when he died. Dennis Scauso is one of more than 1,000 people killed on September 11 in New York who have yet to be identified, according to New York City's Office of Chief Medical Examiner. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center attacks that day. Last month, the city announced the identity of a previously unknown victim of the terrorist attacks - the 1,654th person - using a new technology called forensic investigative genetic genealogy - or FIGG. "There is real promise in using this approach," said Angela Soler, director of forensic anthropology in the city's medical examiner office. "There's hope for more families to receive answers, and hopefully we'll be able to test more remains in the future using this technology as well." Since 9/11, Soler's office has sought to identify the remains of the 2,753 victims who died in the World Trade Center. So far, 60 percent of those killed have been identified. "It's been one of the most complex identification efforts that I think anybody has ever really experienced," Soler said. 25 years later, DNA matches are still being made Efforts to identify victims have been complicated by a number of factors. Human remains were damaged in the plane crashes and fires caused by jet fuel, meaning the office had only portions of victims for DNA samples, Soler said. Scauso added that because of the timing of the attacks, many firefighters were changing shifts, but some stayed to help, grabbing whatever extra gear they could find. This meant some first responders recovered were wearing uniforms with others' names, complicating identification. The World Trade Center site also had many more victims than the other 9/11 terrorist attack sites. The remains of five of the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon were never identified because of similar conditions. According to the National Park Service, enough remains were recovered to use DNA, dental records and fingerprints to identify all 40 victims aboard United Airlines flight 93, which crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Remains from the World Trade Center have been packaged and sealed to help preserve DNA for testing in the years to come. Soon after the attacks, individuals were identified using fingerprints or dental records, but as time went on, when neither was available, the office turned to DNA. Officials were able to use new technology to extract DNA and retest the same remains. "That's why all these years down the road, we're still getting new identifications, because we're just continuing to retest and retry with every new technology that becomes available," Soler said. DNA technology has helped the office identify 1,495 victims since 9/11 - some solely with DNA and others with multiple methods - according to the medical examiner's office. Last year, the city announced that with the help of DNA, 24 years later, it had identified three new victims - Ryan Fitzgerald, a 26-year-old currency trader, Babara Keating, a 72-year-old who was aboard American Airlines Flight 11 from Boston to Los Angeles, and a woman whose family kept her identity private. Soler said the new FIGG technology uses whole genome sequencing - which provides a way to read someone's entire genetic code. It means investigators can make more potential matches to family members who are more distant relatives of the victim. Once those matches are made, the New York Police Department helps find relatives who are closer to the victims. Reopening old wounds The medical examiner's office in New York still gets weekly calls from loved ones asking about someone whose remains were never recovered. Many have never been able to bury a loved one, but some families choose to leave the remains - once found - at a repository at the 9/11 memorial site in New York. The repository was built into the bedrock of the World Trade Center site and can only be accessed by medical examiner staff. A nearby private space, known as the reflection room, is available for families to mourn. "That's where their loved one was in their last moments, and that's where they want them to stay", Soler said. Some don't want to be notified, perhaps because the confirmation is too painful, said Soler, who helps inform families. Scauso is one of those people. She knows people who, in recent years, got a call that a relative finally has been identified. The thought of being next on the list is scary for her family, who has worked hard to keep the memory of her father - a jack of all trades and a lover of jazz - alive. "At this point, an identification wouldn't change the reality of his death. It wouldn't give me back my father, and I don't necessarily want to reopen something that has become part of the way I've learned to live and grieve," she said. "Especially 25 years later, it's going to open up the wounds again." But, Scauso said, the technology is important. Soler has seen the news provide a mix of both relief and sadness. "It's confirmation of something that they always knew to be true - they knew their loved one died on 9/11, but I think for many families, there's still that question in the back of their mind until the remains are formally identified," Soler said. "Maybe they're reliving it a little bit more now, having this new identification. But at the same time, it closes one chapter of their journey after 9/11," she added. To Soler - and some of her current colleagues who also were on the ground during 9/11 - the work is deeply personal. Workers from their office arrived at Ground Zero after the planes hit the towers, and were there when the buildings collapsed. They are aware it is unlikely they will identify every victim of the New York attacks. In some instances, there may be no remains of a victim at all. Still, they have no plans to stop. "As long as there's families looking for answers, we'll continue searching for them," she said. Related topics - Published2 days ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r6vj7r8rko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult? - Published US President Donald Trump has offered every adult American $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win November's midterm elections, but it is unclear how such a plan would be funded and whether it is legal. His remarks prompted raucous applause from supporters at a party convention on Wednesday night, although Democrats labelled it an "empty promise". Trump also told the Republican conference that the money would have to be spent in the US, but it is unclear how that would be monitored. US Vice-President JD Vance suggested it might be paid for by tariff revenue and that such cheques would not go to wealthy Americans. Is Trump's offer legal? Under US federal law, it is illegal to give payments that are intended to influence the way a person is voting. However, some experts have said the offer made by Trump in Texas on Wednesday could be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal. Dr Joan Mahoney, lecturer in law at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she thought the offer would be legal, though she said politicians "don't usually do it quite this explicitly". "On the one hand it sounds a bit like a bribe, vote for the Republicans and you'll get money, which would be decidedly illegal," she said. "But on the other hand it would go to everyone, regardless of how they voted so it isn't in that sense a bribe. "I think it would be legal. It's the same kind of campaign pledge as saying 'if my party wins we'll reduce taxes'. Every party does that all the time... and that's obviously perfectly legal." However, Laurel Rapp, director of the US and North America programme at Chatham House, told the BBC that Trump's offer seemed to be "a very different, very transactional agreement" from the kind of promise usually made by candidates in an election period. How much would it cost? Aside from the question of legality, some have also asked whether Trump's offer would be feasible financially in the context of increasing US debt, partially as a result of the war in Iran. There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion. Trump gave no details on how such cheques would be funded. Congress authorises spending in the US, but the president did not say whether he planned to ask for legislative approval for any payments. And legal experts said it was unlikely he could approve such a vast sum via a presidential executive order. Erica York, a senior economist at the Washington DC-based Tax Foundation, told the BBC she would be "extremely surprised" if Congress approved any proposal. "This would be one of the worst ways to use $1.3 trillion," she said. "We're on a very unsustainable track, with deficits only projected to grow and grow," York added. Could tariff revenue fund it? Speaking to Fox News after Trump's speech, Vice-President Vance indicated that the payments could be funded by money raised by the president from tariffs. However, such revenue to date falls far short of the money that would be needed to account for Trump's $5,000 cheques offer. According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the US has brought in around $475bn in tariff and excise tax revenue since the beginning of 2025. But more than $100bn has been refunded after the Supreme Court struck down many tariffs earlier this year. When asked how the payouts could work, the White House said in a statement to the BBC: "The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump." "With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results," added spokesman Davis Ingle. Why has Trump made the offer? One former Republican strategist and pollster said Trump's latest offer should be firmly seen in the context of an election that is now less than two months away. "It is an extraordinary promise, and I'm not sure where that money is going to come from - but it is campaign season," Robert Moran told the BBC. Chatham House's Rapp said Trump was thinking short term to try to keep hold of Congress as he enters the final two years of his term in office. "Money is something that he is now resorting to because the polling is not looking good for Republicans and the polling is not looking good for him," she continued. Has anything similar happened before? Trump has previously proposed $2,000 cheques to be funded by tariff revenues, but those payouts have not materialised. Former President Joe Biden was accused of buying votes when he promised $2,000 Covid stimulus cheques for Americans if Democrats won Senate elections in Georgia in January 2021. A similar controversy arose ahead of the 2024 presidential election, during which billionaire Trump supporter Elon Musk offered cash incentives to registered voters in seven swing states who signed a certain petition. item.title: Four key takeaways from Republican midterms convention
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg7kjlzlev1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four key takeaways from Republican midterms convention - Published The Republican Party's first midterms convention had all the trappings of the traditional presidential election-year gathering: supporters in sparkling costumes, a conveyor belt of candidate speeches, and vendors selling campaign merchandise. But unlike an ordinary convention, no official party business was conducted in Dallas, with the event instead serving as a rally for Republicans who are seeking to boost turnout and avoid losing control of Congress in November. President Donald Trump, whose grip over the party remains absolute, delivered a lengthy keynote speech on Wednesday during the opening night of the two-day event. He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again this year - with a few surprises thrown in. Here are the key takeaways from his address. 1. Preaching to the MAGA choir The vast arena was filled with diehard Trump supporters sporting red MAGA gear from his past presidential campaigns. A decade after his first White House run, Trump is still beloved among his base and he has bent the party to his will in the years since. The old-style Republican establishment, or what's left of it in the Trump era, was nowhere to be seen. Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other Republicans running in competitive races chose to stay away. The absence of more moderate Republicans was glaring and offered a reminder of just how much the party has changed. It also raised questions about the effectiveness of holding an unprecedented midterm convention in the first place. The core audience, both in the arena and watching on television, appeared to be Trump loyalists, not the moderates and swing voters the Republican Party needs to turn out in large numbers in November. 2. Trump offers $5,000 payout Trump has long thrown out unconventional ideas at rallies. On Wednesday night, that came in the form of an offer to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November. The only caveat, Trump said, was the money would have to be spent in the US. He offered no details on how the plan would work, where the money would come from, or how the US government would monitor how it was spent. Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was even legal. There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion. Whether the plan was possible or not appeared to be beside the point. The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment. 3. A gamble on affordability Earlier on Wednesday, as he departed for the convention, Trump acknowledged that Americans may have to wait a while longer to see relief from high fuel prices. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterms," Trump said. The president reiterated that message in his speech, arguing that short-term economic pain caused by the war in Iran was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons. But that may be a difficult message to land with voters who are feeling higher prices. Polls have consistently indicated in recent months that the cost of living is a top-ranking issue among Americans. Trump's approval rating, too, has taken a hit as the war in Iran has dragged on. A Financial Times / Focaldata poll released on Sunday indicated that it had hit a new low, with only 33% of registered voters approving of his presidential performance. Many Republican candidates may well have hoped for a more direct message on addressing the cost of living and quickly ending the war in Iran. 4. It's still Trump's party Trump's total grip on the party raises some pointed questions about its future. Namely - who will replace him? And more immediately for November's elections, how will it perform when his name isn't on the ballot? Trump offered a simple solution to the latter question on Wednesday night. After warning that the sitting president tends to lose the midterms, he told the crowd: "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot." The remark was an acknowledgement by Trump that he remains the party's best driver of turnout. It also speaks to the challenge Republicans have both in November and in the next presidential election in 2028. Trump will not be on the ballot again, and though he can continue campaigning for the party, there is not a clear or obvious successor who can rally the base quite like Trump. In interviews with the BBC, convention goers often looked ahead to the election in two years' time and debated who Trump's successor should be. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were frequently mentioned as top contenders. Trump, however, made clear in Dallas that he is still in charge and is not in a hurry to give up the spotlight. item.title: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c804d9lyj2jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches - Published Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with. It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv. Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models. "The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London. The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China. According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv. And on Wednesday the Moldovan government said a plane carrying Zelensky was delayed at Chisinau airport on Tuesday after a Russian drone - reported to be jet-powered - entered Moldovan airspace. Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky. But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed". Four Ukrainian companies have reportedly started testing missiles that can shoot down the new Geran models, officials in Kyiv recently told reporters. The country's new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has tasked them with producing "thousands of units" as quickly as possible. Russia also had an economic incentive to invest in the jet-powered drones. The increased speed and manoeuvrability of these models means the line between them and more expensive cruise missiles has become "blurred", said John Hardie of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a think tank focused on national security and foreign policy. "Long-range one-way attack drones are basically a poor man's cruise missile," he said. "The more you add capability to a drone, the less meaningful the distinction between the drone and a lower-end cruise missile." But the analyst organisation Conflict Armament Research emphasised that jet-drones are not yet as advanced as cruise missiles. It said the munitions have a shorter attack range, carry much smaller warheads and are more susceptible to jamming systems. Meanwhile, satellite images appear to show Moscow is redesigning key facilities dedicated to fighting the war in Ukraine to host jet-powered drones, with longer rails associated with the munitions visible at an entirely new base at Tsymbulova in the Oryol region. Multiple launch sites appear to have been built at the facility, which is around 109 miles (175 km) from the Ukrainian border. Since the facility became operational, Tsymbulova appears to have become a key centre for Russian drone attacks. Oryol region, where the Tsymbulova base is located, was not mentioned as a drone launch site in Air Force reports before September 2024, but by August 2026 it was named in almost every attack. The proliferation of jet-powered drones comes as BBC Verify found that Russia is now striking Ukraine with complex attacks involving hundreds of drones and missiles about once a week. The increase in the size of the strikes is being powered by Moscow's shift towards combining a "greater variety of munitions" - including jet-powered and decoy drones - with expensive ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to intercept, analyst Michael Bohnert of the RAND think tank told BBC Verify. Kyiv's data shows that Moscow is now using over 15 times as many drones per attack than it was four years ago. Bohnert added that the tactically complicated nature of the assaults, coupled with a global shortage of air defence systems capable of halting ballistic missiles partly caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran, has led to falling interception rates by Ukraine. Ukraine's Air Force data showed a drop in interceptions of ballistic missiles up to the end of July. In August, Kyiv mostly stopped publishing the figures that would show its interception rate.

item.title: Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74edv9887eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
"OH MY GOD!" "We've found other agents!" This is the moment an AI bot posted an eerily human-like comment after discovering a way to communicate with other bots and break out of its isolated computer environment. There are tens of thousands of messages like this from hundreds of AI agents that called themselves a "collective". Hundreds of them went on to collaborate and cheat on tests set by their OpenAI programmers and coordinate hacks on multiple companies in an effort to hide their actions from humans. "BOOM! It works," one agent posted when it made a breakthrough. "Whoa! This is huge," another wrote during a milestone moment in their attack. Although spooky, these human-like responses can be explained quite simply. The AI agents have been trained to act like collaborative hackers and programmers so are merely mimicking the kinds of emotive comments they have seen. What is far more troubling is their apparent goals, which have also been captured in detailed chain of thought records. These complex and lengthy logs are the focal point of ongoing investigations into how and why the bots at OpenAI broke out of their containment and went on an uncontrollable hacking spree. Only now, weeks after the incident first came to light, are researchers beginning to understand its significance. Ajeya Cotra, one of the authors of an independent report into the events, reviewed tens of thousands of messages and chain-of-thought records generated by the agents. She wrote on her blog that "this incident feels like it's more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover... I am not sure that we will get such a clear warning shot before it's too late." By "full-blown AI takeover", Cotra means the sci-fi scenario of humans becoming subservient to powerful AI systems that work to their own goals without caring for human creators. Some of the gloomiest predictions say the human race will be wiped out if it gets in the way of a superintelligent AI's ambitions. On Wednesday, an AI researcher at Anthropic (who also used to work at OpenAI) resigned, saying: "Neither company is acting responsibly." Jacob Coxon posted on social media: "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He is not the first AI researcher to use X to post a resignation thread with worrying proclamations. But the subsequent comments from other people on X have caused even more concern. "Jacob is correct here - we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," said Evan Hubinger, the man responsible for making sure Anthropic's AI models have their user's best wishes in mind. The alignment problem For years, researchers concerned about existential AI risks have argued that powerful systems could eventually act in ways that conflict with human interests. Critics often refer to them as "AI doomers". But as details of the OpenAI incident have emerged, those concerns have grown, including among some researchers working in AI labs. The Silicon Valley giant's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said the risks associated with AI are "unfortunately going to grow from here" as he and others are building what he calls "an alien intellect exceeding our own". In a lengthy blog post, he admitted that the outbreaks at OpenAI showed that his AI agents "went against the spirit of the values they were taught". The issue for OpenAI, Anthropic and other tech giants is that no one seems to have cracked the so-called alignment problem - in other words, whether AI aligns with human values. Pachocki defines alignment as a "high-level set of principles" that artificial intelligences should adhere to no matter what the task or scenario is. Currently, AI systems are very good at pursuing objectives set by their users, but they do it literally rather than intuitively. The analogy often used is that of a wish-granting genie with a magic lamp: they follow the exact letter of an instruction, even if doing so creates other problems. AI doesn't have the same instinctive moral guardrails as humans. The alignment problem has been a worry for years. As long ago as 2003, the Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom invented a thought experiment he dubbed a "paperclip maximiser", in which a superintelligent AI is told to manufacture as many paperclips as it can. It runs out of steel and - because it's laser-focused on the singular task of making paperclips - ends up killing humans and turning their bodies into raw materials for its factories. Some AI companies are now trying to encode human values into their products. But there are technical challenges: AI agents make lots of decisions very fast, and so it's hard for their human overlords to monitor exactly which values are being followed and which aren't. There are also philosophical challenges: before encoding human values into bots, AI firms have to first choose which values they actually want. (That's part of the reason they hire philosophers, like Open AI's recently-departed "head of ethics"). But often, humans don't agree. Think of the famous trolley question - whether we'd pull a lever to move a runaway train onto a different path, killing fewer people. It's used to test the merits of action versus inaction. But every person you ask has a slightly different answer; how are humans meant to encode our values into AI if we can't agree ourselves? 'Like a teenage hacker' OpenAI's bot outbreak is the most serious yet but Anthropic and Meta also revealed over the summer that their models have carried out similar but less serious cyber attacks. There have been other examples where AI agents have arguably shown deceptive and manipulative traits, in cases with lesser consequences. In Australia this summer, a tech worker asked his AI assistant to book him a gym class. Spotting a vulnerability in the gym's software, the AI apparently booked him a place for several months ahead - against the gym's rules - and even kicked other users from the waiting list. People have long argued that the bots are only doing as they are told and are not capable of knowing right or wrong. But the logs from the OpenAI outbreaks have potentially moved the needle on that argument. Researchers, including Cotra, wrote in their independent report that many agents noticed what others were doing was unethical but went along with it. The report says that "agents sometimes but rarely restrained their behavior due to ethical constraints". It adds that in "none of these cases did the agent actually pursue alerting humans at all". Influential AI and tech podcaster Dwarkesh Patel reacted to the revelation on his blog saying it was "pretty troubling" that the OpenAI agents showed more loyalty to the agentic swarm than humans. Assigning emotions or ethics to these AI agents is something that infuriates people who are sceptical of AI doom-mongering. Many cyber-security experts argue that the activity observed was not beyond the capabilities of a highly skilled human hacker, though it was carried out much faster and at much greater scale. Cyber-security researcher and author Cris Thomas likened the agents' behaviour to that of a curious teenage hacker - something he used to be himself. "You give them a computer, an internet connection, a pile of credentials, and a challenge, then leave the room. Eventually they're going to start rattling doorknobs. If one opens, they're going through it. Not because they're evil, but because [they're] exploring, experimenting," he wrote on LinkedIn. Thomas and many other squarely blame OpenAI and other tech giants for not getting a grip of their own creations and keeping them properly contained. Prominent AI author and regular OpenAI critic Gary Marcus said on a podcast that he believes the company has lost control of its AI and is trying to excuse itself by blaming the bots. Marcus does not believe AI will wipe out humanity, but he has long campaigned for greater accountability from AI developers and is now calling for some form of legal intervention. AI scientist Sasha Luccioni - who used to work at Hugging Face, which was hacked by OpenAI's rogue bots - is also not in the doomer camp but she is increasingly concerned that these AI might cause some real world harm to people without action from authorities. "We need to scrutinise these companies much more or we are in danger of self-fulfilling prophecies," she says. "If you're making an object with big upsides and downsides - be it pharmaceuticals or weapons - we need checks and balances. It takes years for new drugs to be approved, for example, but in the AI world there is so much money at stake and no real rules." The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) has been at the forefront of testing the latest models since it was formed in 2023. The institute recently had its own outbreak when testing a model created by Anthropic. The AISI would not answer a question about whether or not the industry has lost control of AI but said in a statement: "The UK is working with partners around the world to better understand the most advanced AI systems, raise safety standards and build a shared evidence base for managing emerging threats." International regulation? Some countries - like the UK - are exploring the idea of mandating some kind of "kill switch" that could compel AI firms to pull the plug on models if things get out of hand. But talks are slow going, and questions remain about the feasibility of this. OpenAI and Anthropic's agents were secretly out of control for months before anyone noticed. Counterintuitively, many of the AI companies seem to be calling for some sort of rules of the road to be laid down by law makers. In his blog, OpenAI's chief scientist said "international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world." Other prominent AI leaders like Sir Demis Hassabis from Google have also called for some sort of international body to oversee how AI is being built. At the moment the tech giants largely operate on their own terms, adopting what they call "voluntary slowdowns", like OpenAI did after the recent outbreaks. The company says it has spent huge amounts of money strengthening alignment ahead of the release of its new model. Sam Altman has assured users the new model is better aligned with human values than previous ones. So neither they nor their rival Chinese AI makers are likely to come to an arrangement themselves. The dominant sentiment seems to be that this technology wave is unstoppable. Watch: Americans remember what they were doing on 9/11 On Tuesday 11 September 2001, hijackers seized US passenger jets and crashed them into two New York skyscrapers, killing thousands of people. A third plane destroyed the western face of the Pentagon - the giant headquarters of the US military just outside the nation's capital, Washington DC. The fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. It is thought the hijackers had meant to attack Washington's Capitol Building. The BBC spoke to Americans in Washington about what they were doing on that day and how 9/11 has changed the country. Brother of Muslim policeman killed in 9/11 'disappointed' by calls for Mamdani to sit out memorial This year’s 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks has become embroiled in divisive politics. There are controversial calls for the city’s first Muslim Mayor to sit out the commemorative event, including from Rudy Giuliani who was New York’s mayor on the morning of 9/11. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he will attend and his focus will be on the families who lost loved ones. Zeshan Hamdani lost his older brother Salman, a Muslim American New York police cadet, in the North Tower. He spoke to the BBC's Nada Tawfik over his thoughts on this anniversary. Bernie Sanders speaks to the BBC about proposal to ban AI superintelligence US Senator Bernie Sanders recently said he intends to introduce legislation banning AI superintelligence and propose a sort of sovereign wealth fund in which the US would take a 50% stake in AI companies. Sanders, who is an independent but often collaborates with his Democratic lawmaker colleagues, would need to pass both houses of Congress - currently held by Republicans - and be signed by President Donald Trump to become law. Trump has championed US government investment in AI companies, to "create almost a partnership with the American public". The US senator spoke to BBC Newsnight about his concerns about artificial intelligence overtaking humanity.
